strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem: moving medical LLMs from static QA toward strategic multi-turn clinical inquiry and empathetic communication.

Proposes a coherent agentic RL framework combining a multi-agent interactive environment, a two-tiered reward architecture, and an experience repository; the safety-first veto reward is a sensible design choice.
Reports strong results on HealthBench and MAQuE, including an 8B model outperforming much larger open-source medical LLMs on several metrics, which supports parameter efficiency.
Includes human evaluation and detailed appendices with reward specifications, prompts, and case studies, showing meaningful effort toward clinical realism and safety.
The empirical package is broad: two dialogue benchmarks, static QA benchmarks, ablations, scaling studies, and qualitative case analysis.
weaknesses: The central claim that DOCTOR-R1 "outperforms powerful proprietary models" is contradicted by the paper's own results: GPT-o3 scores higher on HealthBench Main (38.91 vs. 36.29) and HealthBench Hard (23.34 vs. 18.73); on Hard, DOCTOR-R1 is also worse than Baichuan-M2-32B (23.68 vs. 18.73). This is overclaiming and cherry-picking.

The GRPO description and Equation 1 are technically incorrect/misleading. The presented listwise softmax objective is not GRPO; GRPO uses group-normalized advantages, a PPO-style probability ratio, clipping, and KL regularization. If the implementation actually followed Eq. 1, the core RL algorithm is mislabeled.

The experience repository has a questionable retrieval condition: Eq. 6 accepts an experience as "good" only if its semantic similarity to the query is below a novelty threshold, which filters out relevant high-similarity experiences. This contradicts the stated goal of providing useful prior trajectories and may hurt retrieval quality. Moreover, the repository is used only to augment prompts rather than integrated into the RL objective, so the "Experiential Agentic RL" framing is overstated.

Evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests, or multiple seeds are reported, despite small benchmark subsets (e.g., 200 MedQA/MMLU questions) and small reported gaps (e.g., HealthBench 36.29 vs. 33.16).

The human evaluation is weak: only five paid annotators without medical training, no inter-annotator agreement, no sample-size or power analysis, and no assessment of diagnostic correctness. It cannot substantiate claims about clinical safety or medical quality.

Static QA gains are anomalous and unexplained: DOCTOR-R1 improves MedQA from 63.50 to 83.50 and MMLU from 70.00 to 85.00, which is implausibly large for dialogue-focused RL alone. This suggests an unmentioned SFT stage, data contamination, or other confounds that must be isolated and reported.

The process reward relies on a Qwen3-8B LLM judge without clinician calibration or validation against expert ratings. Using the same base model for policy, patient simulator, and evaluator may introduce self-reward bias, and reward-hacking risk is acknowledged but not quantitatively analyzed.

Reproducibility is insufficient: no code, model weights, or training data release is mentioned; the SFT stage and data curation are only partially described; experience-retrieval hyperparameters and filtering thresholds are incomplete.

MAQuE results are mixed and do not clearly support overall superiority: DOCTOR-R1 underperforms GPT-4.1 and Baichuan-M2-32B on adherence, coherence, and clarity, while emphasizing only empathy and accuracy.
Ablations are too coarse: only whole components are removed, with no component-wise studies for retrieval stages, reward dimensions, novelty/reward thresholds, or the proposed safety veto mechanism.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: dynamic, multi-turn clinical inquiry rather than only static medical QA.
Combines multiple relevant ideas—multi-agent patient simulation, reinforcement learning, process/outcome rewards, and experience retrieval—into a coherent system pipeline.
Evaluates on two multi-turn medical benchmarks (HealthBench and MAQuE) plus static QA benchmarks, and includes ablations, a human preference study, and case studies.
Reports strong parameter efficiency for an 8B model and shows improvements over its Qwen3-8B base model on several automated metrics and static QA tasks.
Includes an ethics statement, limitations discussion, and system prompts, which are useful for transparency.
weaknesses: Central evaluation claims are overstated and selectively reported. On HealthBench Main, GPT-o3 scores 38.91 versus Doctor-R1's 36.29, and on HealthBench Hard Doctor-R1 (18.73) is below both Baichuan-M2-32B (23.68) and GPT-o3 (23.34). The abstract and introduction omit these comparisons while claiming superiority over proprietary models.

MAQuE results also do not support the broad claim of superiority. Doctor-R1 ties GPT-4.1 on accuracy (60.00), but has much lower Adherence (70.20 vs. 98.00), Coherence (76.20 vs. 86.60), Coverage (38.52 vs. 46.02), and Relevance (87.50 vs. 90.78). The paper highlights only empathy while ignoring these regressions.

The experience retrieval mechanism appears technically inconsistent. Eq. 6 retains experiences whose similarity to the query is below a novelty threshold, which conflicts with the goal of retrieving relevant experiences and contradicts Stage I candidate selection based on similarity. As written, Stage III would filter out the most relevant candidates.

The reward architecture is inconsistently described. The main text specifies eight process-reward dimensions, while the implementation details in the appendix mention five weighted dimensions. This makes the training objective and reported ablations difficult to reproduce or trust.

The GRPO formulation in the preliminaries is non-standard and likely incorrect as a description of GRPO. It is presented as a listwise softmax cross-entropy over chosen/rejected responses rather than the group-relative advantage-based policy-gradient objective normally used by GRPO.

The 'Experiential Agentic RL' contribution is not convincingly differentiated from retrieval-augmented prompting. It is unclear how stored experiences actually change the policy gradient updates rather than simply being prepended to the prompt at rollout time.

Ablations are incomplete. The paper removes process reward and experience retrieval, but does not compare against standard SFT, standard RL without experience retrieval, alternative reward designs, or full component-wise variants. The claim that better inquiry improves decision-making is therefore not causally established.

Evaluation lacks statistical rigor. There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance estimates for the automated benchmarks, making it difficult to know whether small differences are meaningful.

Human evaluation is weak: only five annotators, no medical expertise, no inter-annotator agreement, no sample size or statistical testing, and inconsistent figure labels (e.g., GPT-5 and DeepSeek-v3 appear without clear relation to the main text). This makes the human preference claim unreliable.

The LLM-as-judge reward/evaluator is not quantitatively validated. The same Qwen3-8B family is used for the policy, patient agent, and reward model, raising concerns about reward hacking, self-preference, and evaluation bias.

Reproducibility is limited. Key details such as final training-data size, filtered data composition, data splits, random seeds, compute budget per run, code release, and model weights are missing or unclear. Many implementation choices are under-specified.

The paper contains numerous typos, formatting errors, and inconsistent names/numbers: 'Hodging' instead of 'Hedging', 'HaatoGPT' instead of 'HuatuoGPT', 'Medition' instead of 'Meditron', 'Doctor-R1' vs. 'DOCTOR-R1', and the text says MedQA 83.00 while the table says 83.50. This seriously harms clarity and credibility.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior work. The paper combines existing components—multi-agent simulation, GRPO, LLM-as-judge rewards, and memory/retrieval—without a clear theoretical or algorithmic advance. The claim of being the first to unify clinical inquiry and decision-making is overclaimed.

Data governance and ethics are under-specified. The appendix mentions filtering real clinical dialogues from KaMed, but it is unclear whether these are fully de-identified, licensed, or covered by IRB/ethics review. The ethics statement's blanket claim that no private patient data were used needs clarification.

Static QA evaluation uses only 200 sampled questions on MedQA and MMLU, not the standard full test sets, limiting comparability to prior reported numbers. The apparent improvement over the base model on static QA also raises suspicion of benchmark contamination or tuning effects that are not investigated.

The paper does not adequately support real-world significance. The system is a medical AI prototype, yet safety, uncertainty, failure modes, and deployment risks are addressed only superficially in the limitations section.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: moving beyond static medical QA toward dynamic, multi-turn clinical inquiry and empathetic communication.
Integrates several nontrivial components, including a multi-agent interactive environment, RL training, a two-tiered reward design, and an experience repository, with substantial engineering effort.
Evaluates on multiple relevant benchmarks (HealthBench, MAQuE, MedQA, MMLU) and includes a human preference study; the 8B model shows parameter efficiency on some metrics.
The case study qualitatively illustrates how strategic questioning and safety awareness can matter in high-risk clinical scenarios.
weaknesses: Technical soundness is questionable: the GRPO formulation in Eq. (1) is not the standard GRPO objective, which uses group-normalized advantages and a clipped PPO-style surrogate, not a softmax over rewards. This misrepresents the core optimization algorithm.

The experience retrieval mechanism appears flawed as written: Eq. (6) selects experiences when semantic similarity to the query is below a novelty threshold, which contradicts relevance-based retrieval. It also uses R(E_i) instead of R(E_j), and implementation details are inconsistent (e.g., five vs. eight reward dimensions).

Evaluation claims are overstated and cherry-picked: Doctor-R1 is outperformed by GPT-o3 on HealthBench Main and Hard, and by Baichuan-M2-32B on HealthBench Hard. On MAQuE, it is weaker than baselines on several axes (Coverage, Adherence, Coherence, Clarity), yet the paper claims broad superiority over proprietary and open-source models.
Human evaluation is weak: only five non-medical annotators, no inter-annotator agreement, no statistical significance testing, and metrics do not directly assess medical correctness or safety.

Reproducibility and evaluation validity are insufficient: no code release details, missing prompt/format details for MedQA/MMLU, no contamination analysis, and the large MedQA/MMLU gains from dialogue RL are suspicious and not adequately justified.

Clarity and consistency issues are pervasive: numerous typos, inconsistent terminology/abbreviations, incomplete abstract text, mismatched reward descriptions between main text and appendix, and formatting problems in tables.

strengths: Addresses an important and clinically relevant problem: dynamic multi-turn patient inquiry, empathy, and diagnostic decision-making rather than static medical QA.
Proposes a reasonably comprehensive framework combining multi-agent simulation, two-tiered rewards, GRPO-based RL, and an experience repository, with several ablations and case studies.
Evaluates on multiple relevant benchmarks (HealthBench, MAQuE, MedQA, MMLU) against a wide range of proprietary and open-source medical LLMs, including parameter-efficiency comparisons.
Reports strong gains over open-source specialized models and demonstrates promising patient-centric/communication improvements in human evaluations.
Includes detailed appendices on implementation, prompts, reward design, failure modes, and some human evaluation details, indicating substantial engineering effort.
Provides an ethics statement and reproducibility statement, acknowledging risks and intended research-only use.
weaknesses: The GRPO formulation in Equation 1 is technically incorrect: it presents a listwise contrastive/log-softmax loss, not GRPO. The actual GRPO objective involves group-relative advantages, PPO-style ratio clipping, and KL regularization. This undermines the paper's central algorithmic description.

The claims are overbroad and selectively framed. The paper repeatedly claims superiority over powerful proprietary models, but GPT-5 clearly outperforms Doctor-R1 on HealthBench Main (46.38 vs 36.29), HealthBench Hard (29.57 vs 18.73), and MAQuE accuracy (67 vs 60). GPT-5 is omitted from several abstract/introduction claims, which is misleading.

The reward model validation is weak. The consultation evaluator is a Qwen3-8B model from the same family as the policy, and the reported Spearman correlation with human expert rankings is only about 0.24, which is weak, not 'moderate high' as claimed. The reward signal may therefore be unreliable.

Human evaluation is insufficiently powered: only two licensed physicians, five lay annotators, and small numbers of rated dialogues/cases. No confidence intervals, significance tests, or inter-annotator agreement statistics are reported, making the conclusions fragile.

The experience retrieval mechanism is poorly specified and in places seems inverted. Equation 6 conditions 'good experience' addition on semantic similarity being below a novelty threshold, which is counterintuitive for retrieving relevant experiences. The novelty/reward filtering logic needs clarification and stronger ablation.

The POMDP formalization is loose and arguably incorrect: states are described as patient queries, actions as utterances, and observations as dialogue history, but the resulting MDP-like notation is not rigorously connected to the learning objective.

Novelty is incremental. The paper combines existing ideas (GRPO, multi-agent RL, process rewards, retrieval/memory) with a medical dialogue application. The 'first to unify' claim is questionable given prior agentic medical models such as DoctorAgent-RL and Baichuan-M2 in Table 5.

The evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no error bars, variance estimates, multiple seeds, or significance tests are provided for the main benchmark results. Single-run benchmark differences of a few points may not be meaningful.

Some metrics and results are inconsistent or confusing: e.g., Appendix B says 'five weighted dimensions' while the main text and Table 6 use eight; scaling experiments refer to '100k simulated patient agents' when they likely mean 100k patient cases/dialogues; GPT-5's Empathy score is anomalously low compared with weaker models.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Code/model weights are promised but no actual URLs or release details appear in the manuscript. Training data construction from KaMed and 100k simulated dialogues is not fully specified, and there is no IRB/consent discussion for using real clinical dialogue corpora.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: moving medical LLMs beyond static QA toward dynamic, multi-turn clinical inquiry with empathy and strategic information gathering.

Proposes a coherent high-level pipeline combining multi-agent simulation, process/outcome rewards, GRPO-style optimization, and experience retrieval; the system design is ambitious and clinically motivated.

Reports gains on HealthBench and MAQuE over base models and several open-source/medical baselines, especially on communication quality, context awareness, and empathy, with some parameter-efficiency advantages at 8B scale.
Includes several ablations (process reward, experience retrieval, veto system, soft-skill weights, Llama transferability) and case studies that illustrate failure modes and intended agent behavior.
Provides human evaluation with both patient-perspective annotators and licensed physicians, and includes an ethics/limitations statement and appendix details.
weaknesses: The GRPO formulation is technically incorrect or at least severely misdescribed. Equation 1 is a listwise softmax/contrastive ranking loss, not standard GRPO, which relies on group-normalized advantages and a clipped policy-ratio objective. This undermines the algorithmic claims and the comparison against PPO.

The POMDP formalization is inconsistent and superficial. The state is defined as the patient agent's consultation query rather than the latent clinical condition, transitions are not properly specified, and the observation/reward definitions do not support the claimed formalism.

The experience retrieval mechanism is questionable and possibly inverted. Equation 6 treats an experience as 'good' when its similarity to the query is below a novelty threshold, which could retrieve semantically dissimilar, less relevant experiences. The paper also conflates in-context retrieval with actual policy learning, overstating 'Experiential Agentic RL'.

The reward model is an LLM (Qwen3-8B) of the same scale as the policy, and its validity is not convincingly established. The reported Spearman correlation with human expert rankings is weak (rho > 0.24 on only 40 cases), so the reward signal may be unreliable and could bias both training and ablation conclusions.

Evaluation is incomplete and not fully convincing. On HealthBench Hard, Doctor-R1 is not state-of-the-art and is substantially below Baichuan-M2-32B and GPT-5, contradicting broad SOTA claims. Human evaluation is small in scale (2 physicians, 5 annotators, limited cases) and lacks statistical significance tests or confidence intervals.

Baselines are insufficient for the central claims. Many compared open-source models are weak or outdated, and there is no comparison to strong memory/RAG or agentic dialogue baselines beyond limited similarity/random/state-only variants. This makes the novelty and effectiveness of the experience repository hard to assess.

Novelty is incremental: the framework mostly combines existing ideas—multi-agent simulation, LLM-as-judge rewards, GRPO/RL, process rewards, and retrieval-augmented generation—without a clear fundamental advance.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper claims code and model weights are available but does not provide actual links or artifact identifiers; training data construction from KaMed and GPT-4.1-Nano annotations are not fully released or described.

Several claims are overstated relative to evidence, e.g., 'first' to unify clinical inquiry and decision-making, 'mastering clinical inquiry,' and 'experiential RL' when the experience module mainly prepends retrieved examples to the prompt. The abstract and introduction promise more than the experiments support.

Presentation has inconsistencies and technical typos that hurt clarity, including the incorrect GRPO equation, confusing retrieval filtering conditions, possible score/label mismatches across tables, and a very heavy appendix/main-text imbalance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: moving medical LLMs beyond static QA toward strategic, empathetic multi-turn clinical inquiry.
The proposed Doctor-R1 framework is comprehensive, combining a multi-agent interactive environment, a two-tier reward architecture, and an experience repository within an agentic RL pipeline.

The empirical results on HealthBench Main and MAQuE are promising: an 8B model outperforms several larger open-source specialized models and some proprietary models on key communication and accuracy metrics.

The paper includes extensive ablations (e.g., SFT/PPO/GRPO, reward components, experience retrieval, dialogue turns, patient-agent scaling) and a human evaluation covering patient experience and expert ratings.
The writing is generally clear, and the appendices provide substantial implementation details, case studies, and additional analyses.
weaknesses: The GRPO formulation in Equation 1 is not standard GRPO: it is a listwise softmax/ranking loss without importance ratios, clipping, or group-relative advantages. This is a significant technical misrepresentation of the core optimization algorithm.

The experience retrieval mechanism is conceptually confusing, especially Equation 6: it adds experiences to the repository when their similarity to the query is below a novelty threshold, which contradicts the goal of retrieving relevant experiences for the current state. The intended novelty filtering logic is unclear and likely flawed.

There are inconsistencies in the reward architecture description: the main text says the process reward evaluates eight dimensions, while Appendix B states it evaluates five weighted dimensions. This undermines clarity and reproducibility.

The paper overclaims superiority. For example, on HealthBench Main GPT-5 scores 46.38 versus Doctor-R1's 36.29, and on HealthBench Hard GPT-5 scores 29.57 versus Doctor-R1's 18.73. The abstract and contributions selectively emphasize weaker proprietary baselines while omitting GPT-5's clear advantage.

The human expert evaluation does not clearly support the claim of superior clinical capability: Doctor-R1's average expert score (4.30) is essentially tied with Baichuan-M2-32B (4.31) and only slightly above GPT-5 (4.03), yet the abstract claims superior clinical capability. The patient-experience evaluation is stronger but relies on only five non-expert annotators.

The expert validation uses only two licensed physicians and very limited sample sizes. The reported Spearman correlation with human expert rankings is low (ρ > 0.24), which undercuts confidence in the reliability of the LLM-based reward model used for training.
Main results lack statistical significance tests or confidence intervals, making it difficult to assess whether observed differences are meaningful.
Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of actual code or model-weight links despite the reproducibility statement claiming they are provided.
